modules.description: An arbitrary CQL statement, run as given against one cluster.
modules.name: command

run.description:
Execute a raw CQL statement over the native protocol (imperative verb-action,
no cqlsh and no shell).
By default changed=false (like a probe); the driver cannot tell whether a
statement mutated anything, so declaring it is the author's job — and so is
idempotency, which this action does not provide.

★ params.args WORK ON DML ONLY — SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, BATCH. The
driver prepares only those, and on any other statement it DISCARDS the values
silently, leaving the ? markers unbound and the statement a syntax error. So
args on a non-DML statement are REFUSED here rather than dropped: you get the
reason before the run instead of an unexplained syntax error during it.
On DML, write `WHERE id = ?` with args, never `WHERE id = ${ ... }`.

This is the escape hatch for what the four managed objects deliberately leave
out: GRANT and REVOKE, table options, clustering order, indexes, materialized
views and user-defined types. Those take their values in the statement text,
because the driver will not bind them.
★ THAT MAKES IT THE WRONG PLACE FOR A SECRET. A value written into params.cql
is in the scenario, in the rendered task and in the statement — none of which
the ADR-010 masks cover. Rotating a role password through this action is
therefore NOT supported; see role.present on what this artifact does and does
not manage.

A statement the driver would not prepare may be DDL, so this action WAITS for
schema agreement after it, exactly as the keyspace and table states do.

WARNING (security): rows come back in Output.rows IN PLAINTEXT — that is
Cassandra's answer, not a plugin-managed secret, so it is NOT covered by the
ADR-010 masks. DO NOT read credential tables through this action
(system_auth.roles carries salted_hash). params.password itself is masked and
never reaches the statement or the events (see the guard tests). Values are
rendered as TEXT, because a CQL row holds types an event has no equivalent for;
do not build a comparison on their shape. At most 100 rows are returned and
Output.truncated says when that bound was hit.
No dry-run preview (the plugin does not implement PlanReadSafe).

args.description: Values bound to the statement's ? markers, in order. A whole number arrives as a 64-bit integer, so a column declared int needs a value in its range. ★ Accepted ONLY on a DML statement (SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/BATCH): the driver binds nothing on anything else, so setting this beside a DDL or a GRANT is refused rather than silently ignored.

changed.description: Report the result as changed=true (for a statement that actually mutates). Default false (probe semantics).

cql.description: The CQL statement. One statement — the protocol takes no batch of them separated by semicolons. On DML (SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/BATCH) write ? markers and pass the values in params.args; on anything else the driver binds nothing, so the values go in the statement text — and a secret must therefore never be one of them.

hosts.description: Contact points: a list of "host" or "host:port". The driver discovers the rest of the ring from them, so this is a list and not a single address — two or three nodes is enough, and one is a single point of failure for the connect only.

keyspace.description: Session keyspace, so the statement may name tables unqualified. Optional — a fully qualified <keyspace>.<table> needs none. ★ The session connects INTO it, so a keyspace that does not exist yet fails the connection: create it with keyspace.present first, or fully qualify and leave this unset.

password.description: Password of the connecting role (vault-ref in operator-input; keeper resolves it before Apply). Goes into the connection credentials only — never into a statement, never into events, logs, traces or UI (masked, ADR-010).

port.description: CQL native transport port, applied to any contact point given without one and to the peers the driver discovers. Default 9042.

tls.description: Connect over TLS (client_encryption_options on the node). Default false (plaintext). Declared as a BOOLEAN and refused if written as a string: the insecure side of this parameter is the default, so a coerced value would send the password out in the clear (NIM-778).

tls_ca.description: PEM CA certificate verifying the node certificates (RootCAs). Masked (secret). Resolved keeper-side from Vault during render.

tls_cert.description: PEM client certificate for mTLS (optional, only together with tls_key). Masked (secret).

tls_key.description: PEM client key for mTLS (optional, only together with tls_cert). Masked (secret); does not end up in events or errors.

tls_skip_verify.description: EXPLICIT opt-out of node certificate verification. Default false (verification enabled — default secure).

username.description: Role to authenticate as (PasswordAuthenticator). This is WHO THE STEP CONNECTS AS, not the role a role-action manages (that is params.name).

modules.description: A live Cassandra node: liveness and the version, cluster, datacenter and rack it reports for itself.
modules.name: instance

pinged.description:
Health-probe a Cassandra node over the native CQL protocol (no cqlsh, no shell):
open a session and read system.local. Opening the session already proves TCP,
the CQL handshake and — with credentials — authentication; the query proves the
node is SERVING and not merely accepting connections.
Read-only, changed=false by design (a probe, not a mutation). Output carries
ok plus release_version / cluster_name / data_center / rack / host_id, so a
health gate reads register.self.ok and a version gate reads
register.self.release_version.
No dry-run preview (the plugin does not implement PlanReadSafe).

absent.description:
Drop a keyspace over the native CQL protocol (no cqlsh, no shell), with the
same schema-agreement wait as `present`. Idempotent: a keyspace that is not
there is a no-op (changed=false).

★ DROP KEYSPACE DESTROYS EVERY TABLE AND EVERY ROW IN IT. There is no
confirmation parameter and no dry-run preview (the plugin does not implement
PlanReadSafe): the guard is that a scenario has to name the keyspace to drop it.

present.description:
Converge a keyspace to the declared replication, over the native CQL protocol
(no cqlsh, no shell). The live schema is READ first and one of three things
happens: absent -> CREATE KEYSPACE; already as declared -> no-op (changed=false);
declared differently -> ALTER KEYSPACE. Idempotent: a repeat apply on a converged
keyspace changes nothing and reports changed=false.

SCHEMA AGREEMENT: after its own CREATE or ALTER the state WAITS until every
reachable node reports the same schema version, and fails if they do not reach
it. Cassandra propagates schema through gossip, so a state that reported changed
the moment the statement returned would leave the next step of the run failing on
a keyspace that 'does not exist' on the node it happened to reach.

★ REPAIR IS NOT PART OF THIS STATE. Raising a replication factor changes the
SCHEMA and moves no data: the new replicas hold NOTHING until `nodetool repair`
has run on every node of the affected datacenters. This state does not run it and
does not wait for it — there is no CQL statement for repair (it is a
JMX/nodetool operation that runs for hours on real data), and this plugin speaks
only CQL. Until repair completes, a read at a consistency level the new factor
made reachable can return NO DATA. Output.repair_required is true whenever this
state raised a factor, AND whenever it changed the strategy class — the two
strategies do not share an option vocabulary, so which nodes hold a partition
changes regardless of the numbers. Gate the follow-up on
register.self.repair_required rather than on the step having succeeded.
Lowering a factor instead leaves surplus copies on the former replicas; that is
not a correctness problem, and `nodetool cleanup` reclaims the space when you
choose to.
No dry-run preview (the plugin does not implement PlanReadSafe).

durable_writes.description: Whether writes go through the commit log. Default true. false trades durability for write throughput and is a deliberate choice, never a default.

name.description: Keyspace to converge. Lowercase letters, digits and underscore, starting with a letter or underscore, at most 48 characters. An uppercase name is REFUSED rather than folded: Cassandra lowercases an unquoted identifier, so the state would create it and then never find it again.

absent.description:
Drop a Cassandra role over the native CQL protocol (no cqlsh, no shell).
Idempotent via system_auth.roles: a role that does not exist is a no-op
(changed=false).

Cassandra refuses to drop a role that still owns permissions or is still
granted to another role; that refusal is reported as the failure it is, not
worked around.
No dry-run preview (the plugin does not implement PlanReadSafe).

present.description:
Converge a Cassandra role over the native CQL protocol (no cqlsh, no shell).
system_auth.roles is READ first: absent -> CREATE ROLE; login and superuser
already as declared -> no-op (changed=false); either of them different ->
ALTER ROLE. Idempotent.

★ THE PASSWORD OF AN EXISTING ROLE IS NEITHER READ NOR CHANGED. role_password is
applied only on the CREATE path. Cassandra stores the password as a salted hash,
so it cannot be compared with the declared one, and a state that re-applied it
every run would report changed forever — a state that never converges.
★ ROTATION IS NOT SUPPORTED BY THIS ARTIFACT AT ALL, and command.run is NOT a
way around it: the driver binds no values on an ALTER ROLE, so the password
would have to be written into params.cql — into the scenario, the rendered task
and the statement text, none of which the ADR-010 masks cover. Rotate out of
band until this artifact grows a state that owns it.

On the CREATE path the password IS written into the statement text, because the
driver refuses to bind it there. It never reaches an event, a message or an
error — every failure of this action is redacted — but a cluster with audit or
slow-query logging will record it, which is inherent to Cassandra role
management and true of cqlsh and every other driver.

No schema-agreement wait, deliberately: a role is a ROW in system_auth, not a
schema change, and it does not travel the gossip path keyspace and table DDL do.

Grants are not managed by this object. `GRANT`/`REVOKE` on a keyspace or table
go through command.run.
No dry-run preview (the plugin does not implement PlanReadSafe).

same schema-agreement wait as `present`. Idempotent: a table that is not there
is a no-op (changed=false).

dry-run preview (the plugin does not implement PlanReadSafe).

present.description:
Create a CQL table over the native CQL protocol (no cqlsh, no shell), with the
same schema-agreement wait as keyspace.present: the state does not report
changed until every reachable node holds the new schema, so the next step of the
run cannot fail on a table that 'does not exist'.
system_schema.columns is READ first: absent -> CREATE TABLE; already as declared
-> no-op (changed=false). Idempotent.

★ AN EXISTING TABLE THAT DOES NOT MATCH IS A FAILURE, NOT AN ALTER. Cassandra
cannot change a primary key at all and cannot change a column's type; the only
reconciliation it would accept is adding a column, and a state that added what it
could while ignoring the primary key it could not would report success on a table
that is not the declared one. Dropping and re-creating would be data loss
performed by a converge step. So the state names exactly what differs and stops.
A column the live table has and this declaration does not is NOT a difference —
the declaration is the columns this service needs, not the complete set the table
may carry.

TABLE OPTIONS ARE NOT MANAGED: compaction, compression, gc_grace_seconds,
default_time_to_live and caching are neither set nor compared. A table needing
them is created with command.run. There is deliberately no options parameter,
because one that applied only at CREATE would silently do nothing on a table that
already exists.
No dry-run preview (the plugin does not implement PlanReadSafe).

clustering_key.description: Clustering columns, in order. Optional. Clustering ORDER is not managed (the table is created with the default ascending order); a table needing DESC is created with command.run.

columns.description: Columns as a map of name to CQL type: {id: uuid, created_at: timestamp, tags: "map<text, text>"}. Every column named by partition_key or clustering_key must appear here.

hosts.description: Contact points: a list of "host" or "host:port". The driver discovers the rest of the ring from them, so this is a list and not a single address — two or three nodes is enough, and one is a single point of failure for the connect only.

keyspace.description: Keyspace the table lives in. NOT a session keyspace: statements fully qualify <keyspace>.<table>, so a keyspace that does not exist yet is reported by CREATE TABLE rather than failing the connection.

name.description: Table to converge. Lowercase letters, digits and underscore, starting with a letter or underscore, at most 48 characters.

partition_key.description: Partition key columns, in order — the composite partition key ((a, b)) when there is more than one. Must name at least one column: a Cassandra table has no default primary key.
